analysis.one_liner: Lets gun violence victims sue gun manufacturers and dealers by repealing the industry's special immunity from lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a 24-18 vote in July 2022 but never received a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, a federal law — the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act — has barred most lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers, sellers, and dealers for harm caused when their products are criminally misused. No other consumer industry has this kind of blanket protection: if a car, a drug, or a tool is used to hurt someone, victims can go to court. This bill would repeal that shield and also let victims' lawyers use ATF gun-trace data — which currently cannot be used in civil cases — as evidence in court. The House Judiciary Committee approved it 24-18, but the full House never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who would regain the ability to sue gun manufacturers, dealers, and sellers in court for harm caused by criminal or unlawful misuse of firearms — the same access to the courts they have against makers of cars, drugs, and other products. Attorneys general and cities pursuing litigation over illegal gun distribution would also regain a tool, since the bill makes ATF gun-trace data usable as evidence in civil suits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of gun violence and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 2-4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which currently prohibits civil actions against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm. After repeal, victims could sue in state or federal court on the same basis as they can sue other industries.

Makes ATF firearms trace data subject to subpoena and discovery, admissible as evidence, and usable in any civil action or administrative proceeding. Victims and their lawyers could use this data to show where a crime gun came from and whether a dealer had a pattern of problematic sales.

Creates the possibility of financial accountability for manufacturers and sellers whose distribution practices supply illegal markets, similar to the litigation pressure that has changed conduct in the tobacco, opioid, and automotive industries.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, sellers, and their trade associations, which would face civil lawsuits and litigation costs over criminal misuse of firearms they lawfully sold — costs that could partly be passed to buyers through higher prices or fewer dealers.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the PLCAA would expose gun makers, dealers, and sellers to civil lawsuits over the criminal misuse of firearms by third parties — conduct by people they may never have met. Supporters of the immunity law argue that holding lawful sellers liable for others' crimes raises costs and risks driving small dealers out of business, and some of those costs could show up in prices for legal buyers.

A wave of litigation is an indirect tool: it works through years of discovery, settlements, and court costs rather than through any clear rule, so the outcome for victims would vary case by case and could take many years to produce changes in industry conduct.

Opening the ATF firearms trace database to discovery in civil suits would put sensitive law-enforcement trace information into the hands of private litigants, which law-enforcement agencies have historically resisted because of concerns about revealing investigative sources and methods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: for two decades, people harmed by gun violence have been unable to use the courts against the gun trade the way they can against car, drug, and other product makers, and trace data that could show patterns of illegal sales has been sealed away from them. Repeal would restore equal access to the courts, and evidence-based lawsuits target negligent sellers rather than lawful owners. The costs are serious and worth naming honestly: sellers of a lawful product would face expensive litigation over crimes committed by third parties, some marginal dealers could close, and gun prices could rise — effects that fall hardest on small-town shops and on buyers, not on the large manufacturers. Critics also warn of litigation designed to bankrupt the industry rather than compensate genuine victims. Whether those costs are worth restoring victims' day in court is the core judgment the bill asked Congress to make; the House never made it.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in July 2022, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 22, 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its Crime Subcommittee in October 2021, where it sat for nine months.
On July 20, 2022, the subcommittee was discharged and the full committee marked up the bill, voting 24-18 to order it reported with amendments.
The committee reported the bill on July 26, 2022 (H. Rept. 117-436) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting a floor vote.

No floor vote ever followed. The bill sat on the calendar until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and bills not passed by then die and must start over from introduction in the next Congress.
All 86 supporters — the sponsor and 85 cosponsors — were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations keep the federal immunity from lawsuits that the bill would have repealed, and victims of gun violence remain unable to sue the gun industry the way they can sue other product makers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry, which keeps its lawsuit immunity

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: all 85 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the committee vote to advance the bill was 24-18, with the no votes coming from committee Republicans.

industries.note: The bill repeals the federal immunity that has shielded them from civil suits over criminal misuse of their products since 2005. Victims' lawsuits could reach manufacturers through negligent-distribution and marketing claims, creating litigation costs and settlement exposure that do not exist today.

Retailers and dealers would lose immunity from suits over straw purchases and negligent sales, and could be forced in discovery to turn over sales records using the newly available ATF trace data. Compliance and litigation costs would fall hardest on small dealers.

Trade associations are named defendants under the current immunity law and would lose that shield along with the industry, facing suits over lobbying and marketing activity. Their political advocacy helped win the immunity in 2005 and opposed its repeal.
